html:
An outbreak of measles in Fiji in 1875 that killed tens of thousands of people, by most estimates between a quarter and a third of all Fijians.

Fiji had just become a British colony, in October 1874. Early in 1875 the chief Cakobau and his party came home from a visit to Sydney on a British warship. Some of them had measles. The ship was not quarantined, and soon after, chiefs from across the islands gathered for a large meeting and carried the disease home.

Fijians had never met measles and had no immunity. Whole villages fell ill at once, with no one left well enough to fetch food and water. Many died of hunger and neglect as much as of the virus.

The disaster shaped the colony. The new governor, Arthur Gordon, wanted to protect Fijian village life and did not want Fijians worked on plantations. With fewer people to work the land, he turned to India, and from 1879 shipped in indentured Indian workers. A similar tragedy struck Samoa with the 1918 flu.
sum: An outbreak of measles in Fiji in 1875 that killed tens of thousands of people, by most estimates between a quarter and a third of all Fijians.
